f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: Ethiopia's Afar State is home to about 1.8 million Afar people, by a government projection.
In 2008 Afar pastoralists set up the Afar Pastoralist Council so they could raise their voices at regional, national and international level.

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: In Eritrea, the Afar are one of at least four Indigenous peoples, who have lived in their traditional territories for about two thousand years.

n.l: the Afar region of north-eastern Ethiopia, the Dankalia coast of Eritrea, and Djibouti

f.t: Anywaa activists helped found EMIPRO in 2022, the first legally registered Indigenous-led rights organization in Ethiopia.
The Anywaa are river farmers and fishers whose lives follow the Akobo, Alwaro, Openo (Baro) and Gilo rivers of Gambella.

n.l: Gambella in western Ethiopia, along the Akobo, Alwaro, Openo (Baro) and Gilo rivers, and neighbouring South Sudan

f.t: The M'Zab valley habitat, built in the tenth century by the Ibadites around five ksour (fortified towns), survives intact and is UNESCO World Heritage.
UNESCO notes the egalitarian principle carefully applied by Mozabite society, seen in architecture designed for community living.
UNESCO credits the M'Zab with an ingenious system for capturing and sharing water which, with its palm groves, makes life work in a semi-desert.

n.l: the M'Zab valley around Ghardaïa in the Algerian Sahara

f.t: BaAka singing is four-voice polyphony mastered by the whole community. UNESCO first recognized it in 2003 and inscribed it on its heritage list in 2008.

n.l: forests between the Oubangui and Sangha rivers, in south-western Central African Republic and northern Republic of the Congo

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: Bagyeli and Bakola communities live across about 12,000 km2 of southern Cameroon, especially around Akom II, Bipindi, Kribi and Lolodorf.
In late 2018 Bagyeli communities filed three Community Forest applications with Cameroon's forestry ministry, after mapping their own forest use.

n.l: the forests of southern Cameroon, around Akom II, Bipindi, Kribi and Lolodorf

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: A 2021 agreement signed with the Baka association ASBABUK gives Baka communities around Lobéké National Park access for their traditional activities in the park.

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: In Gabon, the Baka are one of nine Indigenous forest peoples, alongside the Babongo, Bakoya and others, each with its own language and culture.

n.l: forests of eastern and southern Cameroon, northern Gabon, and neighbouring parts of the Republic of the Congo and Central African Republic

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: In May 2023 Uganda's Office of the Prime Minister directed the wildlife authority (UWA) to stop evictions of Benet communities.
In 2005 Uganda's High Court recognized the Benet as the historical, indigenous inhabitants of Mount Elgon, a landmark land-rights ruling.

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: The Mosopisyek Benet have lived on Mount Elgon in Uganda for more than five hundred years.

n.l: the slopes of Mount Elgon in eastern Uganda, in Kween, Kapchorwa and Bukwo districts

f.t: The Endorois Welfare Council, founded in 1995 by senior members of the community, works for justice and sustainable development for the Endorois.

n.l: around Lake Bogoria in Baringo County, and in Nakuru and Laikipia counties, in Kenya's Rift Valley

f.t: Early Griqua communities governed themselves through leaders called kaptyns, with magistrates drawn from leading families.
Klaarwater, the settlement Griqua people founded, later took the name Griquatown.

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: Griqua communities live today in the Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape, Free State and KwaZulu-Natal.

n.l: the Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape, Free State and KwaZulu-Natal provinces of South Africa

f.t: In July 2026 Namibia's Vice President opened a high-level meeting in Outjo with the Hai//om Traditional Authority on a development plan for Hai//om communities.

f.p: Cultural Survival (by the Hai//om Community San Council)
f.t: Many Hai//om communities lived on lands that are now Etosha National Park and the surrounding regions, according to the Hai//om Community San Council.

f.p: Cultural Survival (by the Hai//om Community San Council)
f.t: Hai//om heritage includes their own language, storytelling, music and traditional knowledge, and the council calls for mother-tongue teaching in early grades.

n.l: north-central Namibia, in and around Etosha National Park and on resettlement farms in Kunene, Oshikoto and Oshana regions

f.p: Congrès Mondial Amazigh / Amazigh World Congress
f.t: Each 30 August, Amazigh Flag Day marks the flag's adoption in 1997 by Amazigh representatives from across North Africa and the diaspora.

n.l: North Africa (Tamazgha): Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and Egypt's Siwa oasis, with communities across the Sahel and in the diaspora

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: Kabyles make up around half of Algeria's Amazigh population, centred on Kabylia in the north-east.

f.p: Inalco (Institut national des langues et civilisations orientales)
f.t: Taqbaylit, the Kabyle language, is one of three Amazigh languages taught from bachelor's level to doctorate at Inalco in Paris.

n.l: Kabylia in north-eastern Algeria, with a large community in France

f.t: Nationwide, 3.2% of Morocco's population reported Tarifit among the local languages they use, in the 2024 census.
In Morocco's 2024 census, 53.6% of people in Al Hoceima province said they use Tarifit, the language of the Irifiyen.

n.l: the Rif of northern and north-eastern Morocco, including Al Hoceima province

f.p: Haut-Commissariat au Plan (HCP), Direction Régionale de Souss Massa
f.t: In the Souss-Massa region, 63.2% of residents use Tachelhit, the language of the Ishelhin, according to Morocco's 2024 census.
Nationwide, 14.2% of Morocco's population reported Tachelhit among the local languages they use, in the 2024 census.

f.p: Inalco (Institut national des langues et civilisations orientales)
f.t: Tachelhit, the language of the Ishelhin of southern Morocco, is one of three Amazigh languages taught at Inalco in Paris.

n.l: the Souss valley, the Anti-Atlas and the western High Atlas of south-western Morocco

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: The Karimojong, whose economy has long rested on livestock, live mainly in the drylands of north-eastern Uganda, about 1.09 million people in a 2018 estimate.

f.p: Kara-Tunga (partner of Cross Cultural Foundation Uganda)
f.t: Cultural Heritage Clubs in five secondary schools in Napak and Moroto treat heritage as central to Karimojong history and identity.

n.l: the Karamoja drylands of north-eastern Uganda

f.t: Imzad music, played by Kel Tamasheq (Tuareg) women on a one-string bowed instrument they craft from a gourd, has been on UNESCO's heritage list since 2013.

n.l: the Sahara and Sahel: northern Mali and Niger, southern Algeria and Libya, and northern Burkina Faso

f.t: The Khoisan revival is an ongoing cultural, social and academic movement in South Africa, centred on identity and reclaiming history.

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: Many South Africans once classed as Coloured under apartheid now identify as Khoikhoi or San, exercising their right to self-identification.

n.l: South Africa, especially the Western, Northern and Eastern Cape, including Nama, Griqua and Korana communities

f.t: The Konso built the dry-stone terraces of their highlands and still farm them; UNESCO lists the Konso Cultural Landscape as World Heritage.
The Konso raise stone steles to mark the handing of responsibility from the older generation to the younger, a living tradition.
In Konso walled towns, communal spaces called moras keep a central place in community life.

n.l: the Konso highlands of south-western Ethiopia

f.t: In their own !Ora language, the Korana's name for themselves is !Orakua or !Orana.

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: Korana communities live mainly in Kimberley and in the Free State province.
People in Bloemfontein active in the Khoisan revival have raised the idea of bringing the Kora (!Ora) language back into use.

n.l: Kimberley and the Free State province, South Africa

f.t: Mbuti and Efe peoples live in the Okapi Wildlife Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in the Ituri forest, which is essential to their economy and culture.
UNESCO calls for ensuring the involvement of the Indigenous Mbuti and Efe peoples in the management of the Okapi Wildlife Reserve.

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: The Mbuti, with the Baka and Batwa, are widely acknowledged as the first inhabitants of the DR Congo's rainforests.

n.l: the Ituri forest of north-eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo

f.t: In South Africa's Richtersveld, Nama families still build portable rush-mat houses called haru oms and move herds between seasonal grazing grounds.

n.l: southern Namibia and the Richtersveld and Namaqualand areas of South Africa's Northern Cape, with smaller communities in Botswana

f.t: OPDP set the 7th annual Ogiek Cultural Event for 14 August 2026 at Nkareta, Narok, themed on how Ogiek traditions thrive and adapt amid change.

n.l: highland forests of Kenya, especially the Mau Forest

f.t: UNESCO lists the Gada system as an indigenous democratic socio-political system of the Oromo, inscribed on its heritage list in 2016.
Gada, the Oromo system of governance, is organized in five classes, and leadership rotates from one class to the next every eight years.
Knowledge of the Gada system is passed on to Oromo children today, at home and at school.

n.l: Oromia and other regions of Ethiopia, and northern Kenya

f.t: All of Reteti's elephant keepers come from the Samburu community and are formally trained to care for, rehabilitate and release elephant calves.
Reteti in Namunyak Conservancy, set up at the local Samburu community's request, calls itself the world's first Indigenous community-owned African elephant sanctuary.
With support from the Samburu Women's Trust, Samburu women are exercising land rights: 20 women and three women's groups own land in one home area.
The Samburu Women's Trust trains Samburu women on their constitutional rights and helps them share their views with government.

n.l: Samburu County and nearby rangelands of north-central Kenya

f.t: Nyae Nyae, a homeland of mostly Ju|'hoansi communities, became Namibia's first communal conservancy in 1998.
When Ju|'hoansi formed their farmers' cooperative, they began with open consensus meetings, then elected two representatives per community, at least one of them a woman.

n.l: Nyae Nyae and the Tsumkwe area of north-eastern Namibia, and neighbouring north-western Botswana

f.t: ǂKhomani people have won back cultural rights in South Africa's Kalahari Gemsbok National Park, such as using its resources and hunting in traditional ways across much of it.
The ǂKhomani are actively reclaiming their knowledge and traditions. Their Kalahari homeland became a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape in 2017.
At the community-owned Imbewu bush camp, young ǂKhomani learn from elders about plants, animals and the land in a field school called veldskool.

n.l: the southern Kalahari in South Africa's Northern Cape, including the Kalahari Gemsbok National Park near the borders with Botswana and Namibia

f.t: XK FM, a public radio station in Platfontein, South Africa, is the only station in the country that broadcasts in the Khwe and !Xun languages.

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: In South Africa, Khwe and !Xun communities live mainly at Platfontein, near Kimberley.

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: In Namibia's Zambezi Region, Khwe San communities live in and around Bwabwata National Park.

n.l: north-eastern Namibia, north-western Botswana and southern Angola, and Platfontein near Kimberley in South Africa

f.t: XK FM, a public station first on air in 2000, now broadcasts from Platfontein about 15 hours a day in the !Xun and Khwe languages.

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: In South Africa, !Xun and Khwe communities live mainly at Platfontein, near Kimberley.

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: The !Xun are one of Namibia's San peoples, each of which speaks its own language and keeps distinct customs and histories.

n.l: north-eastern Namibia and southern Angola, and Platfontein near Kimberley in South Africa

f.t: Siwa is the easternmost outpost of Tamazgha, the lands traditionally home to Amazigh peoples.
A sense of Berber belonging has revived in Siwa this century; a letter of the Tifinagh alphabet, the Amazigh symbol, now names a bazaar below old Shali.
Ten Siwan tribes speak Siwi, an eastern Amazigh (Berber) language, in the oases of Siwa and El-Gara.

n.l: the oases of Siwa and El-Gara in Egypt's Western Desert, near the border with Libya

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: About 50,000 Toubou live in Libya along the border with Chad; the people's origins lie in the Tibesti plateau.

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: Toubou herders practise mobile pastoralism across a wide area stretching from northern Niger to Sudan.

n.l: the Tibesti plateau of northern Chad, southern Libya along the Chad border, and northern Niger

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: Zimbabwe's 2013 Constitution lists Koisan among its 16 languages, and in 2023 the Tsoro-o-tso San Development Trust worked on the Tjwao language.

f.p: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)
f.t: About 3,207 Tshwa live in Zimbabwe, where they self-identify as an Indigenous people, mostly in the western districts.

n.l: Tsholotsho and Bulilimamangwe districts of western Zimbabwe

f.t: In 2008 thousands of Wodaabe herders attended the fourth General Assembly of the Woodaabe Pastoralists of Niger.
Cattle herding is the main livelihood of the Wodaabe, who move with the seasons across the Sahel.

f.p: MSH Mondes (CNRS and Université Paris Nanterre)
f.t: Each year thousands of Wodaabe gather in Niger's Sahel for a great ceremonial meeting whose central event, the geerewol, is held in song and dance.

n.l: the Sahel of Niger, with communities in Chad, northern Cameroon and north-east Nigeria

f.p: International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED)
f.t: Yiaku women and elders now lead language teaching and forest care, and growing youth involvement is strengthening the community.

f.p: International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED)
f.t: Since 2003 the Yiaku Laikipiak Trust has worked to protect Mukogodo Forest and keep Yiaku culture alive.

n.l: Mukogodo Forest in Laikipia County, Kenya
